title: Trump says he's working on a 'fair' trade deal with Canada

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump, flanked by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, right, and Vice-President JD Vance, speaks during a news conference Friday at the White House. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

blocks.text: World

In a news conference at the White House on Friday after returning from his trip to Asia that included a brief meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney, U.S. President Donald Trump floated the prospect of reaching a trade deal with Canada soon — but said more work needs to be done to get there.
'While more work remains to be done with Canada, Prime Minister Carney was very nice,' Trump tells reporters
U.S. President Donald Trump floated the prospect of reaching a trade deal with Canada soon but said more work needs to be done to get there.

In a news conference at the White House on Friday after returning from his trip to Asia that included a brief meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney, Trump said he's working on a trade deal with Canada.

"While more work remains to be done with Canada, Prime Minister Carney was very nice," Trump told reporters. "One of the things he wants to do is build a Keystone pipeline for us — and we like that. But, you know, got to do a lot more than that."

Trump repeated several of his most frequently stated grievances, claiming Canada has been ripping off the U.S. for years and insisting his country doesn't need energy, vehicles or lumber from its northern neighbour.

items: 'If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy,' Carney says of ongoing trade talks

blocks.text: "That being said, we're working on making a deal that's fair," Trump continued.

The U.S. president complained about the trade deficit with Canada, and put the figure at "about $80 billion." That's closer to the actual 2025 goods trade deficit of $48 billion US than the $200-billion figure he has often used.
"I said, when it's down to zero, come over and let's start talking," Trump said.
Trump's comments come as the Carney government seeks an interim agreement with the U.S. aimed at bringing down some of the most onerous tariffs on Canadian exports.
Canada pursues tariff relief through interim U.S. trade deal

Ottawa's negotiators are looking for an end to the 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian exports that the Trump administration imposed in August, as well as relief from sectoral tariffs that have crippled Canada's steel, aluminum, auto and forest industries.

They are also hoping to stave off Trump's threat to jack up tariffs on vehicles and auto parts to 50 per cent on Jan. 1. While that deadline is now just six weeks away, the U.S. has not filed any formal notice about the threat, which the president made in a social media post in August.
'Move the ball forward'
Trump held his news conference with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice-President JD Vance at his side.
In his own remarks, Rubio spoke of "unfairness and imbalance" in commercial relations with Canada.

items: Reaching interim U.S. trade agreement would kickstart new CUSMA talks, minister says

blocks.text: "The president had an opportunity to visit with the prime minister and move the ball forward on getting to a final agreement that is good for American workers and fair to the United States of America," Rubio said.
Chris Galdieri, a professor of political science at Saint Anselm College in Manchester, N.H., said he believes striking a trade deal that brings stability is in the interests of both countries now.
"It's clear that the tariffs against Canada have not had the effect that Trump wanted them to," Galdieri told CBC News Network on Friday.

"I think he thought that these would instantly bring in a flood of money, cause no pain to anybody in the U.S — certainly not to U.S. consumers — and cause Canada to be brought to heel by the power of the tariffs. That hasn't happened," Galdieri said.
"If you had some sort of durable agreement, at least for the rest of Trump's presidency, it would probably let him feel like he could declare victory and move on."

items: Carney meets with Trump at APEC, says Canada's trade with China isn't U.S. president's top concern

blocks.text: On Wednesday, Carney told the New York Times' DealBook summit that Canada and the U.S. had made progress toward an agreement in recent weeks, but cautioned, "We're not there yet."

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc told the CBC's Power & Politics on Thursday that an interim deal with the Trump administration would likely include some level of Section 232 tariffs on steel, aluminum, auto and lumber — albeit at lower rates.
'If you can get an interim deal, I'd take it'

Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware says getting rid of the 50 per cent tariffs that Trump imposed in August would be a significant accomplishment for Canada that could be followed by more after the Democrats take control of Congress in January.
"Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal for the long term," Coons told CBC's Power & Politics on Friday.
"We need Congress to call Trump to account, to stop insulting our trusted and valued allies and partners in Canada."

This was Trump's first full-fledged news conference since the sweeping midterm elections defeat two weeks ago that saw his Republican Party lose control of both the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives.
Data centre backlash is a problem for Trump’s Republicans
He floated another out-of-the-blue policy that could have implications for Canada's efforts to attract artificial intelligence investment from U.S. tech giants.
Without providing any details, Trump said U.S. companies will face an unspecified tax if they build their AI data centres abroad.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," he said. "We're going to put a tremendous tax on them if they do it."

It's unclear what impact Trump's proposal — which he said he had not revealed to his senior staff — would have on two major data centre projects in Canada backed by U.S. tech giants Meta and Anthropic.

items: Want to build a data centre in Canada? These are the federal government's new expectations

blocks.text: Meta announced in July that it plans to invest $13 billion to build a massive data centre northeast of Edmonton, its first such project in Canada.
Anthropic said in October that it has taken a 20-year lease on a data centre in its pre-construction phase in Cape Breton.
The proliferation of data centres in the U.S. became an issue in the midterms, with both registered Democrats and Republicans mobilizing against such construction in their communities.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
